eLife posts the editorial decision letter and author response on a selection of the published articles (subject to the approval of the authors). An edited version of the letter sent to the authors after peer review is shown, indicating the substantive concerns or comments; minor concerns are not usually shown. Reviewers have the opportunity to discuss the decision before the letter is sent (see review process). Similarly, the author response typically shows only responses to the major concerns raised by the reviewers.

Thank you for choosing to send your work entitled “Decoding the neural mechanisms of human tool use” for consideration at eLife. Your article has been evaluated by a Senior editor and 3 reviewers, one of whom is a member of our Board of Reviewing Editors.

The following individuals responsible for the peer review of your submission want to reveal their identity: Dora Angelaki (Reviewing editor) and Brad Mahon (peer reviewer).

The Reviewing editor and the other reviewers discussed their comments before we reached this decision, and the Reviewing editor has assembled the following comments to help you prepare a revised submission.

The paper is clearly written and organized, and tackles an important question with a well-thought-out and sophisticated approach. Overall this is excellent work, although there are some concerns/questions that the authors should address:

1) An aspect of the Results that is not sufficiently brought out up front in the article (Abstract and Introduction) is that in different regions it is possible to distinguish different factors within the experiment. For instance, the fact that in pMTG upcoming actions can be decoded only when they are performed with the tools, whereas in Superior parietal-occipital cortex decoding was higher for the hand than for the tool, is a really important aspect of the findings that is somewhat buried. The authors should bring this out more fully.

2) It seems somewhat surprising that the regions able to decode across effector (tool→hand, hand→tool) are in IPS and premotor cortex, while regions within IPS/premotor cortex were also shown to have better decoding for hand than for tools. How can the authors reconcile these different effects (are they different populations of voxels driving the decoding accuracy?). Perhaps plotting the weights, voxel-wise, could help to address this.

3) It would be good to see the results (e.g., in figure form, and reduced statistics) for the control analysis of decoding of the ventricle and outside of the brain. This analysis addresses a really insidious issue that will be at the forefront of skeptical readers’ minds; it should be dealt with in full (rather than just saying the analysis was performed and there were no effects).

4) In discussing the occipital-temporal decoding of upcoming actions, the authors come close to, but shy away from, considering whether the organization of the ventral stream may be constrained by the way that the ventral stream is connected up with the rest of the brain (e.g., specificity for the visual representations of body parts could be driven by connectivity to regions of somatosensory or motor areas, and the same for regions that represent tools). The authors’ findings, showing that occipital temporal regions can decode upcoming actions would seem to resonate with that type of an explanation of the causes of neural specificity for different classes of visual stimuli in the ventral stream, at least as it applies to the representation of tools.

5) The auditory cue to determine the subjects’ movement seems to have been the same for both the hand and tool conditions. This consistency across effectors could be responsible for some or even all of the apparently cross-effector classification. That is, the activity in the ROIs that show above-chance cross-effector decoding of actions could be due to the content of the cue rather than preparation for the action per se. This issue must be addressed.

6) It was not clear that the authors balanced the number of voxels across ROIs. This is potentially important as other studies have shown that MVPA performance is strongly influenced by the number of voxels tested.

7) The authors averaged across both directions of the cross-effector test (hand→tool and tool→hand). It is possible however that there are asymmetries in action coding that would be revealed by disentangling these tests.

8) While the authors find that the univariate response properties of regions generally correspond to decoding performance with MVPA, this could partly reflect the ROI approach that was used. A whole-brain MVPA mapping approach might well reveal other regions that code action preparation that are not activated (or not selectively activated) in the univariate sense.

9) The authors note the increased sensitivity of their method relative to a univariate approach, but MVPA (like any other method) carries assumptions and limitations that should shape how the data are interpreted. This could be discussed.

10) The authors report MVPA analyses at each time point, yet we did not find much in the discussion of the results about how these decoding effects develop over time.

claims.evidence_reasoning: This describes a critical feature of the experimental manipulation.

claims.claim: Multi-voxel pattern analysis was used to decode preparatory (pre-movement) signals.
claims.source_text: Using multi-voxel pattern analysis (MVPA) to decode preparatory (pre-movement) signals, we then probed exactly where in frontoparietal cortex and in tool- and body-selective areas in occipitotemporal cortex movement plans (grasping vs reaching) for the hand and tool were distinct (effector-specific) vs where signals related to upcoming actions of the hand could be used to predict the same actions performed with the tool (effector-independent).
claims.evidence_reasoning: This describes the analytical method used in the study.

claims.claim: The delayed-movement task included a Preview phase of 6 seconds where subjects had vision of the target object but were unaware of which action to perform.
claims.source_text: Trials began with the 3D object being illuminated while the subject maintained fixation (Preview phase; 6 s).
claims.evidence_reasoning: This describes the experimental task timing and structure.

claims.claim: The Plan phase lasted 12 seconds after subjects were instructed which movement to perform.
claims.source_text: Subjects were then instructed via headphones to perform one of two movements: Grasp the object ('Grasp') without lifting it or Touch the object ('Touch'), initiating the Plan phase portion of the trial. Following a fixed delay interval (12 s)
claims.evidence_reasoning: This describes the experimental task timing and structure.

claims.claim: The contrast of movement generation vs visual object presentation revealed activity throughout a well-documented frontoparietal network of areas.
claims.source_text: This [Plan & Execute > 2*Preview] contrast revealed activity throughout a well-documented frontoparietal network of areas
claims.evidence_reasoning: This is an experimental finding that is consistent with established literature.

claims.claim: The extrastriate body area has been widely implicated in coding perceptual functions related to the body.
claims.source_text: One area of interest, EBA, has been widely implicated in coding perceptual functions related to the body, including the identification of other individuals, the processing of others' emotional states and movements, as well as perception of the self and representations of the body schema
claims.evidence_reasoning: This is supported by cited literature on EBA function.

claims.claim: Posterior middle temporal gyrus has been implicated in coding numerous perceptual functions related to tools.
claims.source_text: Likewise, pMTG has been implicated in coding numerous perceptual functions related to tools, including tool motion, identification, naming, auditory processing, and the retrieval of semantic information concerning their use
claims.evidence_reasoning: This is supported by cited literature on pMTG function.

claims.claim: Both EBA and pMTG are activated by self-generated movements.
claims.source_text: Interestingly, both ROIs are also activated by self-generated movements (unseen hand actions in the case of EBA and pantomimed tool actions in the case of pMTG; Lewis, 2006; Frey, 2007; Downing and Peelen, 2011).
claims.evidence_reasoning: This is supported by cited literature showing motor-related activation in these regions.

claims.claim: Predictive movement information generally arises in the two time points prior to initiation of the movement.
claims.source_text: First, predictive movement information, if it is to emerge, generally arises in the two time points prior to initiation of the movement
claims.evidence_reasoning: This is an observation from the time-resolved decoding analysis.

claims.claim: Accurate classification never arises prior to the subject being aware of which action to execute.
claims.source_text: Second, in support of the notion that this predictive motor information is directly related to the 'intention' to make a movement, accurate classification never arises prior to the subject being aware of which action to execute (i.e., prior to the auditory instruction delivered at the initiation of the Plan phase).
claims.evidence_reasoning: This is an observation from the time-resolved decoding analysis that supports the interpretation of intention-related signals.

claims.claim: Decoding related to movement planning can be fully disentangled from decoding related to movement execution.
claims.source_text: Finally, decoding related to the planning of a movement can be fully disentangled from decoding related to movement execution, which generally arises several imaging volumes later.
claims.evidence_reasoning: This is an observation from the time-resolved decoding analysis.

claims.claim: SPOC and EBA coded planned actions with the hand but not the tool.
claims.source_text: Some regions (SPOC and EBA) coded planned actions with the hand but not the tool (areas in red).
claims.evidence_reasoning: This is a direct experimental finding from the MVPA analysis.

claims.claim: SMG and MTG coded planned actions with the tool but not the hand.
claims.source_text: Some regions (SMG and MTG) coded planned actions with the tool but not the hand (areas in blue).
claims.evidence_reasoning: This is a direct experimental finding from the MVPA analysis.

claims.claim: Anterior intraparietal sulcus and motor cortex coded planned actions with both effectors but did so using different neural representations.
claims.source_text: Other regions (aIPS and M1) coded planned actions with both effectors (areas in pink) but did so using different neural representations.
claims.evidence_reasoning: This is a direct experimental finding from the MVPA and cross-decoding analysis.

claims.claim: Posterior IPS, PMd and PMv coded the final type of action to be performed with invariance as to whether the hand or tool was to be used.
claims.source_text: A final set of brain areas (pIPS, PMd and PMv) instead coded the final type of action to be performed with invariance as to whether the hand or tool was to be used (areas in purple).
claims.evidence_reasoning: This is a direct experimental finding from the cross-decoding analysis.

claims.claim: In SPOC, decoding accuracies for the hand were significantly higher than for the tool and for across-effector decoding.
claims.source_text: in L-SPOC, decoding accuracies for the hand were significantly higher than for the tool and for across-effector decoding (both at p<0.05; F1.538 = 6.084, p=0.014)
claims.evidence_reasoning: This is a statistical result from the repeated-measures ANOVA analysis.

claims.claim: In SMG, decoding accuracies for the tool were significantly higher than for the hand and for across-effector decoding.
claims.source_text: in L-SMG, decoding accuracies for the tool were significantly higher than for the hand and for across-effector decoding (both at p<0.05; F1.959 = 10.016, p<0.001)
claims.evidence_reasoning: This is a statistical result from the repeated-measures ANOVA analysis.

claims.claim: In motor cortex, decoding accuracies for the hand were significantly higher than across-effector decoding.
claims.source_text: in L-motor cortex, decoding accuracies for the hand were significantly higher than across-effector decoding (p<0.05; F1.398 = 6.239, p=0.016)
claims.evidence_reasoning: This is a statistical result from the repeated-measures ANOVA analysis.

claims.claim: In pMTG, decoding accuracies for the tool were significantly higher than for the hand.
claims.source_text: and lastly, in L-pMTG, decoding accuracies for the tool were significantly higher than for the hand (p=0.049; F1.968 = 4.171, p=0.037)
claims.evidence_reasoning: This is a statistical result from the repeated-measures ANOVA analysis.

claims.claim: Visual inspection of the voxel weightings failed to reveal any structured or consistent topography within or across subjects.
claims.source_text: Visual inspection of the voxel weightings failed to reveal any structured or consistent topography within or across subjects
claims.evidence_reasoning: This is an observation from the voxel weight analysis.

claims.claim: Voxels coding for one particular type of action tended to spatially cluster.
claims.source_text: Note that the only consistency observed was that voxels coding for one particular type of action [as indicated by the positive or negative direction of the weight] tended to spatially cluster
claims.evidence_reasoning: This is an observation from the voxel weight analysis.

claims.claim: Accurate across-effector classification in Heschl's gyrus arises distinctly earlier in the Plan-phase compared to frontoparietal areas.
claims.source_text: We found that although accurate across-effector classification does indeed arise in Heschl's gyrus during the trial, it does so distinctly earlier in the Plan-phase compared to that of the frontoparietal areas
claims.evidence_reasoning: This is a direct experimental finding from the auditory cortex control analysis.

claims.claim: The temporal disconnect between cross-decoding in Heschl's gyrus and frontoparietal cortex makes it unlikely that effector-invariant responses in frontoparietal cortex are fully attributable to auditory commonalities in the planning cues.
claims.source_text: The temporal disconnect between the cross-decoding found in Heschl's gyrus (which emerges in the fourth volume of the Plan-phase) and frontoparietal cortex (which generally emerges in the fifth-sixth volumes of the Plan-phase) makes it unlikely that the effector-invariant nature of the responses revealed in PPC and premotor cortex can be fully attributable to simple auditory commonalities in the planning cues.
claims.evidence_reasoning: This is inferred from the temporal pattern of decoding results in auditory cortex versus frontoparietal cortex.

claims.claim: Accurate decoding in a region points to underlying differences in the neural representations associated with different experimental conditions.
claims.source_text: It is worth emphasizing that while accurate decoding in a region points to underlying differences in the neural representations associated with different experimental conditions
claims.evidence_reasoning: This is a general principle of MVPA methodology established in the field.

claims.claim: A lack of decoding can reflect that the region is not recruited for the conditions being compared, contains neural differences that cannot be discriminated by the algorithm, or is similarly engaged in those conditions.
claims.source_text: a lack of decoding or 'null effect' (i.e., 50% chance classification) can either reflect that the region 1) is not recruited for the conditions being compared, 2) contains neural/pattern differences between the conditions but which cannot be discriminated by the pattern classification algorithm employed (i.e., a limit of methodology, see Pereira et al., 2009; Pereira and Botvinick, 2011), or 3) is similarly (but non-discriminately) engaged in those conditions.
claims.evidence_reasoning: This is a methodological consideration in MVPA interpretation supported by cited literature.

claims.claim: SS-cortex activity only discriminates between grasp vs reach movements following movement onset during the Execute phase of the trial.
claims.source_text: For instance, SS-cortex is widely considered to be a lower-level sensory structure and thus anticipated to only show discrimination related to the motor task once the hand's mechanoreceptors have been stimulated at object contact (either through the hand directly or through the tool, indirectly). Accordingly, here we find that SS-cortex activity only discriminates between grasp vs reach movements following movement onset (i.e., during the Execute phase of the trial).
claims.evidence_reasoning: This experimental finding is consistent with the known sensory function of SS-cortex.

claims.claim: Motor cortex shows decoding for upcoming hand- and tool-related actions but no resulting across-effector classification.
claims.source_text: Likewise, in motor cortex we show decoding for upcoming hand- and tool-related actions but, importantly, find no resulting across-effector classification.
claims.evidence_reasoning: This is a direct experimental finding from the MVPA analysis.

claims.claim: The lack of across-effector classification in motor cortex is consistent with the coding of differences in hand kinematics required to operate the tool vs hand alone.
claims.source_text: This latter result is highly consistent with the coding of differences in the hand kinematics required to operate the tool vs hand alone and accords with the presumed role of motor cortex in generating muscle-related activity
claims.evidence_reasoning: This interpretation is inferred from the experimental results and is consistent with cited literature on motor cortex function.

claims.claim: Hierarchical theories of motor control distinguish between various levels of abstraction required for action planning.
claims.source_text: Hierarchical theories of motor control have existed for more than a century (Jackson, 1889; Sherrington, 1906; Hebb, 1949), distinguishing between the various levels of abstraction required for action planning—for example, at the level of muscles, joints, motor kinematics, and movement goals.
claims.evidence_reasoning: This is established theory in motor control supported by historical citations.

claims.claim: SPOC and EBA fail to incorporate tools into the body schema.
claims.source_text: Although typically associated with visual-perceptual processing, EBA, like SPOC, has been implicated in coding movements of the hand/arm (Astafiev et al., 2004; Orlov et al., 2010, although see Peelen and Downing, 2005) and the fact that we were unable to decode tool movement plans from these regions suggests that they fail to incorporate tools into the body schema
claims.evidence_reasoning: This is inferred from the inability to decode tool movements in these hand-selective regions.

claims.claim: SMG and pMTG are typically activated when human subjects view or pantomime tool-related actions.
claims.source_text: SMG and pMTG, in contrast, are typically activated when human subjects view (Lewis, 2006; Peeters et al., 2009) or pantomime (Johnson-Frey et al., 2005) tool-related actions
claims.evidence_reasoning: This is supported by cited literature on tool-related brain activation.

claims.claim: Damage to SMG and pMTG creates difficulty in pantomiming or performing tool use actions.
claims.source_text: and damage to these areas creates difficulty in pantomiming or performing tool use actions (Haaland et al., 2000).
claims.evidence_reasoning: This is supported by cited neuropsychological literature.

claims.claim: Planning-related signals in SMG and pMTG are able to predict real tool actions.
claims.source_text: That planning-related signals in SMG and pMTG are able to 'predict' real tool actions, as shown here, provides an important extension of these previous findings
claims.evidence_reasoning: This is a direct experimental finding that extends previous literature.

claims.claim: SMG and pMTG play an important and selective role in generating object-directed tool actions.
claims.source_text: demonstrating that these areas also play an important and selective role in generating object-directed tool actions.
claims.evidence_reasoning: This is inferred from the tool-selective decoding results in these regions.

claims.claim: Effector-specific action planning in anterior parietal regions and motor cortex provides coding for the kinematic properties and/or dynamics associated with each effector.
claims.source_text: When considering the particular tool used here—where the operating mechanics of the tool were opposite to those of the hand alone—this effector-specific level of action planning is imperative. It provides a coding for the kinematic properties and/or dynamics associated with each effector
claims.evidence_reasoning: This is inferred from the pattern of decoding results in these regions given the experimental design.

claims.claim: Motor cortex provides the largest source of descending motor commands to the spinal neurons that produce hand kinematics.
claims.source_text: These features match the known properties of motor cortex; it provides the largest source of descending motor commands to the spinal neurons that produce hand kinematics (Porter and Lemon, 1993)
claims.evidence_reasoning: This is established knowledge about motor cortex function supported by citation.

claims.claim: Much of motor cortex activity can be accounted for in muscle control terms.
claims.source_text: and correspondingly, much of its activity can be accounted for in muscle control terms (see Kalaska, 2009; Churchland et al., 2012; Lillicrap and Scott, 2013).
claims.evidence_reasoning: This is supported by cited literature on motor cortex function.

claims.claim: Anterior intraparietal sulcus has been strongly implicated in grasp planning and execution.
claims.source_text: In parietal cortex, aIPS has been strongly implicated in grasp planning and execution (e.g., Murata et al., 2000; Culham et al., 2003).
claims.evidence_reasoning: This is supported by cited literature on aIPS function.

claims.claim: Anterior intraparietal sulcus has been implicated in tool use.
claims.source_text: Notably, it has also been implicated in tool use (Gallivan et al., 2009; Jacobs et al., 2010)
claims.evidence_reasoning: This is supported by cited literature on aIPS involvement in tool use.

claims.claim: The anterior IPS is recruited in the planning of tool actions in addition to those of the hand.
claims.source_text: First, the anterior IPS is recruited in the planning of tool actions in addition to those of the hand, suggestive of an important role in preparing actions with both effectors.
claims.evidence_reasoning: This is a direct experimental finding from the decoding analysis.

claims.claim: Hand and tool action representations in anterior IPS may differ depending on the specifics of the kinematics or object-effector interactions.
claims.source_text: Second, this pattern of findings on its own does not demonstrate that hand and tool actions rely on the same underlying representations, as previously interpreted (e.g., Rijntjes et al., 1999; Castiello et al., 2000). Rather, as indicated by our cross-classification findings, the representations may differ, perhaps depending on the specifics of the kinematics or object-effector interactions.
claims.evidence_reasoning: This is inferred from the lack of cross-decoding in aIPS despite decoding for both effectors.

claims.claim: The posterior IPS serves a variety of high-level visual-motor- and cognitive-related functions.
claims.source_text: In the human and macaque monkey, the posterior IPS appears to serve a variety of high-level visual-motor- and cognitive-related functions, such as integrating target- and effector-related information for movement (Andersen and Buneo, 2002) and encoding 3D features of objects for hand actions (Sakata et al., 1998).
claims.evidence_reasoning: This is supported by cited literature on posterior IPS function.

claims.claim: Effector-independent responses in posterior IPS may emerge due to a common coding of object features that are more relevant for grasping than reaching.
claims.source_text: One possibility, in line with this previous work, is that effector-independent responses in these areas emerge due to a common coding of object features that are more relevant for grasping than reaching.
claims.evidence_reasoning: This is a speculative interpretation of the cross-decoding results based on known functions of posterior IPS.

claims.claim: The same set of object features pertinent for grasping with the hand are pertinent for grasping with the tool.
claims.source_text: That is, the same set of object features pertinent for grasping with the hand (object contact points, orientation, distribution of mass, etc.) are pertinent for grasping with the tool
claims.evidence_reasoning: This is a logical inference about the task demands for grasping with different effectors.

claims.claim: PMd and PMv are engaged in hand actions in both the monkey and human.
claims.source_text: We also found evidence for these same types of effector-independent representations in premotor areas, PMd and PMv. Each area is engaged in hand actions in both the monkey (Rizzolatti and Luppino, 2001; Raos et al., 2004, 2006) and human (Davare et al., 2006; Gallivan et al., 2011)
claims.evidence_reasoning: This is supported by cited literature across species.

claims.claim: PMd and PMv are implicated in higher-level goal-related processing.
claims.source_text: and their implication in higher-level goal-related processing (Rizzolatti and Luppino, 2001; Cisek et al., 2003), particularly in the case of tool use with PMv (Umilta et al., 2008), strongly resonates with the findings reported here.
claims.evidence_reasoning: This is supported by cited literature and is consistent with the current experimental findings.

claims.claim: Nearly all fMRI studies examining action-centred coding have adopted tasks that require the observation of others' actions.
claims.source_text: To date, nearly all fMRI studies examining action-centred coding have done so by adopting tasks that require the observation of others' actions (Lewis, 2006; Grafton and Hamilton, 2007; Peeters et al., 2009; Valyear and Culham, 2010)
claims.evidence_reasoning: This is a summary of the existing literature as supported by citations.

claims.claim: Mirror-neurons in the monkey are located in inferior parietal and ventral premotor cortex.
claims.source_text: This particular line of research has been primarily motivated by the discovery of 'mirror-neurons' in the monkey (Rizzolatti et al., 2001), located in inferior parietal and ventral premotor cortex (Fogassi et al., 2005; Umilta et al., 2008)
claims.evidence_reasoning: This is supported by cited neurophysiological literature.

claims.claim: Mirror-neurons discharge both when the monkey performs a motor act and when the monkey views the same act performed by another individual.
claims.source_text: which discharge both when the monkey performs a motor act and when the monkey views the same act performed by another individual.
claims.evidence_reasoning: This is the defining characteristic of mirror neurons as established in cited literature.

claims.claim: There is a strong coupling between the categorical-selectivity of a brain region as defined through visual-perceptual processing and its specific role in behavior as defined through movement planning.
claims.source_text: Here we provide compelling evidence for a strong coupling between the categorical-selectivity of a brain region, as defined through visual-perceptual processing, and its specific role in behavior, as defined through movement planning.
claims.evidence_reasoning: This is inferred from the matching of visual-perceptual selectivity and motor planning selectivity in EBA and pMTG.

claims.claim: The preparatory activity in body-selective EBA and tool-selective pMTG decoded movement plans for hand and tool actions, respectively.
claims.source_text: For instance, in occipitotemporal cortex we found that the preparatory activity in the independently localized body-selective EBA and the tool-selective pMTG decoded movement plans for hand and tool actions, respectively.
claims.evidence_reasoning: This is a direct experimental finding from the MVPA analysis.

claims.claim: Hand- and tool-related actions at certain cortical processing levels may recruit distinct neural populations.
claims.source_text: This indicates that, similar to the highly modular nature of visual-perceptual processing in occipitotemporal cortex (Downing et al., 2006; Kanwisher, 2010), hand- and tool-related actions at certain cortical processing levels may also recruit distinct neural populations.
claims.evidence_reasoning: This is inferred from the effector-specific decoding in occipitotemporal cortex.

claims.claim: Upcoming movements for both the hand and tool could be decoded from the independently defined tool-selective t-aIPS.
claims.source_text: As an interesting departure from these occipitotemporal cortex results, we found that we could decode upcoming movements for 'both' the hand and tool from the independently defined tool-selective t-aIPS.
claims.evidence_reasoning: This is a direct experimental finding from the MVPA analysis.

claims.claim: The decoding of tool actions in t-aIPS is congruent with its activation in observation-based tool-related tasks.
claims.source_text: At the functional level, the decoding of tool actions in t-aIPS is entirely congruent with its activation in observation-based tool-related tasks (for reviews, see Lewis, 2006; Frey, 2007)
claims.evidence_reasoning: The experimental finding is consistent with cited literature on t-aIPS function.

claims.claim: The decoding of hand actions in t-aIPS accords with its close proximity to parietal areas involved in hand preshaping and manipulation.
claims.source_text: and, at the anatomical level, the decoding of hand actions in t-aIPS accords with its close proximity to parietal areas involved in hand preshaping and manipulation (Culham et al., 2003; Valyear et al., 2007; Gallivan et al., 2011).
claims.evidence_reasoning: The experimental finding is consistent with anatomical relationships described in cited literature.

claims.claim: Hand and tool movement planning may only begin recruiting similar neural structures at the level of parietal cortex.
claims.source_text: When compared to the findings in occipitotemporal cortex, this result indicates that hand and tool movement planning may only begin recruiting similar neural structures at the level of parietal cortex.
claims.evidence_reasoning: This is inferred from comparing the effector-specific results in occipitotemporal cortex with the results in parietal cortex.

claims.claim: The decoding of planned hand- and tool-related actions in EBA and pMTG indicates that these signals reflect the intention to perform a motor act rather than sensory feedback responses.
claims.source_text: Although others have shown that hand/arm movements can activate different regions in occipitotemporal cortex (Astafiev et al., 2004; Filimon et al., 2009; Cavina-Pratesi et al., 2010; Oosterhof et al., 2010; Orlov et al., 2010), here we demonstrate that these signals reflect the 'intention' to perform a motor act rather than the sensory feedback responses (visual, proprioceptive, tactile) that accompany it.
claims.evidence_reasoning: This is inferred from the timing of the decoding during the planning phase before movement execution.

claims.claim: EBA and pMTG may play a significant role in action planning and control by predicting the sensory consequences of actions/movement before those consequences unfold.
claims.source_text: This distinction is important because it indicates that these occipitotemporal cortex areas may play a significant role in action planning and control, possibly by predicting the sensory consequences of actions/movement even before those consequences unfold.
claims.evidence_reasoning: This is a speculative interpretation of the planning-related signals in these regions based on forward model theories.

claims.claim: Forward-state estimation is featured prominently in models of action control.
claims.source_text: Given the delay of incoming sensory signals, this type of forward-state estimation is featured prominently in models of action control (Wolpert and Ghahramani, 2000; Wolpert and Flanagan, 2001)
claims.evidence_reasoning: This is established theory in motor control supported by citations.

claims.claim: Predicting the sensory consequences of movement can be used to disambiguate movements of the body (self) vs movements of the world (others).
claims.source_text: and, from the standpoint of perception, predicting the sensory consequences of movement can be used to disambiguate movements of the body (self) vs movements of the world (others) (von Helmohltz, 1866).
claims.evidence_reasoning: This is established theory supported by historical citation.

claims.claim: Forward-state estimations at the level of occipitotemporal cortex remain linked to the type of effector to be used in an upcoming movement.
claims.source_text: The current findings would suggest that such forward-state estimations, at least at the level of occipitotemporal cortex, remain linked to the type of effector (hand vs tool) to be used in an upcoming movement.
claims.evidence_reasoning: This is inferred from the effector-specific decoding in occipitotemporal cortex.

claims.claim: Hand- and tool-related action plans can be decoded from preparatory signals in body- and tool-selective occipitotemporal cortex areas.
claims.source_text: Updating the considerably simpler notion that action planning, particularly in the case of tool use, merely involves 'access' to ventral stream resources (Milner and Goodale, 1995; Valyear and Culham, 2010), these findings show that hand- and tool-related action plans can actually be decoded from preparatory signals in body- and tool-selective occipitotemporal cortex areas.
claims.evidence_reasoning: This is a direct experimental finding that updates previous theoretical frameworks.

claims.claim: The findings suggest a role for occipitotemporal cortex in visual-motor planning.
claims.source_text: In addition to suggesting a role for OTC in visual-motor planning, these findings might also shed light on the organizing principles of the ventral visual stream.
claims.evidence_reasoning: This is inferred from the motor planning-related signals found in occipitotemporal cortex.

claims.claim: Several theories have been proposed to account for the categorical-selectivity of responses throughout occipitotemporal cortex.
claims.source_text: Several theories have been proposed to account for the categorical-selectivity of responses throughout OTC (e.g., for faces, scenes, bodies, tools, etc), with the majority arguing that this modular arrangement arises due to similarities/differences in the visual structure of the world and/or how it is experienced (Kanwisher, 2010).
claims.evidence_reasoning: This is a summary of existing theoretical frameworks supported by citation.

claims.claim: According to one view, faces and scenes activate different regions of occipitotemporal cortex due to underlying visual field preferences.
claims.source_text: For example, according to one prominent view, faces and scenes activate different regions of OTC due to underlying visual field preferences (i.e., faces activate areas with stronger foveal representations, like FFA, whereas scenes activate areas with stronger peripheral representations, like PPA; Levy et al., 2001).
claims.evidence_reasoning: This is a specific theoretical view supported by citation.

claims.claim: According to another view, similarity in visual shape/form is mapped onto ventral temporal cortex.
claims.source_text: According to another well-known view, it is instead similarity in visual shape/form that is mapped onto ventral temporal cortex (Haxby et al., 2001).
claims.evidence_reasoning: This is a specific theoretical view supported by citation.

claims.claim: One view argues that the organization of occipitotemporal cortex emerges as a by-product of the distinct connectivity patterns of occipitotemporal areas with downstream motor structures.
claims.source_text: One particularly compelling alternative view, however, argues that the organization of OTC may be largely invariant to bottom-up visual properties and that it instead emerges as a by-product of the distinct connectivity patterns of OTC areas with the rest of the brain, particularly the downstream motor structures that use the visual information processed in OTC to plan movements of the body (Mahon et al., 2007; Mahon and Caramazza, 2009, 2011).
claims.evidence_reasoning: This is a specific theoretical view supported by citations.

claims.claim: The neural specificity for visual presentation of body parts and tools in occipitotemporal cortex may reflect their anatomical connectivity with frontoparietal areas involved in generating movements and manipulating tools.
claims.source_text: Under this view, the neural specificity frequently observed for the visual presentation of body parts and/or tools in particular regions of OTC may reflect, to a certain extent, their anatomical connectivity with frontoparietal areas involved in generating movements of the body and/or interacting with and manipulating tools, respectively
claims.evidence_reasoning: This is a theoretical interpretation based on cited connectivity framework.

claims.claim: Areas involved in body part- and tool-related processing show 'downstream' functional connectivity patterns.
claims.source_text: a notion that garners some empirical support from the 'downstream' functional connectivity patterns of areas involved in body part- and tool-related processing (Mahon et al., 2007; Bracci et al., 2012).
claims.evidence_reasoning: This is supported by cited functional connectivity studies.

claims.claim: The matching object-selective and planning-related responses within EBA and pMTG resonates with neurophysiological findings in macaque parietal cortex.
claims.source_text: This compatibility of visual- and motor-related responses within single brain areas resonates with neurophysiological findings in macaque parietal cortex showing that the visual-response selectivity of neurons in AIP (for size, shape, orientation, etc.) are often matched to their motor-response selectivity during action (e.g., Murata et al., 2000).
claims.evidence_reasoning: The experimental findings are consistent with cited neurophysiological literature.

claims.claim: The coupling of visual and motor selectivity is thought to mediate the transformation of visual information regarding physical object properties into corresponding motor programs for grasping or use.
claims.source_text: This coupling is thought to mediate the transformation of visual information regarding physical object properties into corresponding motor programs for grasping or use (Jeannerod et al., 1995; Rizzolatti and Luppino, 2001)
claims.evidence_reasoning: This is a theoretical interpretation supported by citations.

claims.claim: The coupling of visual and motor selectivity resonates with the concept of motor affordances.
claims.source_text: and resonates with the broader concept of motor affordances, whereby the properties of objects linked to action are automatically represented in movement-related areas of the brain (Cisek, 2007; Cisek and Kalaska, 2010).
claims.evidence_reasoning: This is a theoretical connection supported by citations.

claims.claim: The findings provide novel evidence suggesting that the specificity of visual object categorical responses in occipitotemporal cortex are linked to a specific role in preparing related motor behaviors.
claims.source_text: our results provide novel evidence suggesting that the specificity of visual object categorical responses in OTC are in some way linked to a specific role in preparing related motor behaviors.
claims.evidence_reasoning: This is a novel interpretation inferred from the experimental findings.

claims.claim: A reverse set of tongs was chosen because it provided an opposite mapping between the proximal movements of the hand and the distal movements of the tool.
claims.source_text: We chose a reverse set of tongs as the tool to be used in this experiment because it provided an opposite mapping between the proximal movements of the hand and the distal movements of the tool (i.e., when the hand closed on the reverse tongs, the end of the tongs opened, and vice versa).
claims.evidence_reasoning: This describes a critical methodological choice in the experimental design.

claims.claim: The reverse tongs manipulation allowed the object-directed motor plans for both effectors to be held constant while uncoupling the lower-level hand kinematics required to operate each effector.
claims.source_text: This incongruence was imperative to the aims of the study (i.e., decoding planned actions independent of the specific muscle activations required) because it allowed the object-directed motor plans for both effectors (hand and tool) to be held constant across the experiment (i.e., grasping or reaching), while at the same time, uncoupling the lower-level hand kinematics required to operate each effector.

results.result_reasoning: The main finding that tool use involves both effector-specific and effector-independent neural representations is well-supported by converging MVPA decoding results across multiple brain regions. The hierarchical organization showing hand-specific coding in SPOC/EBA, tool-specific coding in SMG/pMTG, effector-specific coding in aIPS/M1, and effector-independent coding in pIPS/PMd/PMv is demonstrated with appropriate statistical tests and controls.

The experimental design and methodology are clearly described and appropriate for testing the hypotheses. The use of reverse tongs to dissociate hand kinematics from action goals is a critical and well-justified manipulation. Sample size (n=13), task design with delayed movement paradigm, and MVPA approach are all adequately documented.

Statistical comparisons between decoding accuracies across regions are appropriately conducted using repeated-measures ANOVA with FDR correction. The findings of significantly higher hand decoding in SPOC, tool decoding in SMG and pMTG, and hand decoding in motor cortex are supported by the reported statistics (p-values and F-statistics).

Time-resolved decoding analyses demonstrate that predictive movement information emerges in the two time points prior to movement initiation, only after instruction delivery, and can be temporally separated from execution-related signals. These temporal characteristics support the interpretation that the decoded signals reflect motor intentions rather than sensory feedback or execution.

The auditory cortex control analysis effectively addresses the alternative explanation that cross-decoding results reflect auditory cue similarities rather than motor planning. The temporal dissociation between Heschl's gyrus cross-decoding (4th volume) and frontoparietal cross-decoding (5th-6th volumes) provides strong evidence against this confound.

The control analyses in SS-cortex and motor cortex provide important validation of the MVPA approach. SS-cortex showing only execution-phase decoding confirms sensory processing expectations, while motor cortex showing effector-specific but not effector-independent coding is consistent with its role in generating muscle-specific commands.

The finding that body-selective EBA and tool-selective pMTG decode hand and tool movement plans respectively demonstrates a strong coupling between perceptual selectivity and motor planning. The timing of decoding during the planning phase (before movement execution) supports the interpretation that these signals reflect motor intentions rather than sensory feedback.

The voxel weight analysis reveals spatial clustering of action-selective voxels but no consistent topography across subjects or conditions. While the authors provide reasonable explanations (low decoding accuracies, trial-to-trial variability), the lack of structured patterns limits mechanistic interpretation of how effector-independent coding emerges at the voxel level.

The interpretations regarding functional roles of different regions (SPOC/EBA failing to incorporate tools, SMG/pMTG playing selective roles in tool actions, aIPS coding kinematics for both effectors) are well-supported by the pattern of decoding results and are consistent with prior literature on these regions' functions.

The proposed mechanisms for effector-independent coding (common object features for grasping) and the role of EBA/pMTG in forward-state estimation are speculative interpretations. While plausible and consistent with the data, these claims require additional experiments (e.g., manipulating object features, testing predictive coding directly) to be definitively supported.

The finding that tool-selective t-aIPS decodes both hand and tool movements is well-supported by the data and provides important evidence that hand and tool planning begin recruiting similar neural structures at the parietal level. This contrasts appropriately with the effector-specific findings in occipitotemporal cortex.

The ROI localization using the [Plan & Execute > 2*Preview] contrast is appropriate and reveals activation in well-documented frontoparietal regions. This orthogonal contrast ensures ROI selection is unbiased with respect to the specific experimental conditions being decoded.

Reviewers acknowledge these effector-specific findings as 'a really important aspect of the findings' but note they are 'somewhat buried' in the presentation (Comment 1). The reviewers request better highlighting of these results in the Abstract and Introduction, indicating acceptance of the findings themselves while requesting improved presentation.

Reviewers express concern about the cross-effector decoding findings, noting it 'seems somewhat surprising' that IPS and premotor cortex show both cross-effector decoding and effector-specific preferences (Comment 2). They request voxel-wise weight analysis to determine if 'different populations of voxels' drive these effects, indicating uncertainty about whether the effector-independent coding is genuine or reflects mixed populations.

Reviewers raise a critical concern that 'the auditory cue to determine the subjects' movement seems to have been the same for both the hand and tool conditions' and state 'this consistency across effectors could be responsible for some or even all of the apparently cross-effector classification' (Comment 5). While the authors present temporal disconnect evidence, reviewers state 'this issue must be addressed,' indicating substantial uncertainty about whether cross-effector decoding reflects motor planning or auditory cue processing.

Reviewers note that 'the authors report MVPA analyses at each time point, yet we did not find much in the discussion of the results about how these decoding effects develop over time' (Comment 10). Additionally, they request that 'MVPA (like any other method) carries assumptions and limitations that should shape how the data are interpreted' be discussed (Comment 9), indicating the temporal dynamics and methodological interpretation require clarification.

Reviewers request voxel-wise weight plotting to address whether 'different populations of voxels' drive different decoding effects (Comment 2). The manuscript reports lack of consistent topography, but reviewers seek this analysis to reconcile seemingly contradictory findings, suggesting uncertainty about the spatial organization of the representations.

Reviewers note that 'the authors' findings, showing that occipital temporal regions can decode upcoming actions would seem to resonate with' connectivity-based explanations of ventral stream organization (Comment 4). They encourage the authors to develop this interpretation more fully, indicating acceptance of the occipitotemporal motor planning findings while requesting deeper theoretical discussion.

Reviewers describe the paper as 'clearly written and organized' that 'tackles an important question with a well-thought-out and sophisticated approach' and state 'overall this is excellent work.' These main conclusions about hierarchical and distributed representations are implicitly accepted through this general endorsement, though specific methodological concerns are raised about particular aspects of the evidence.

Reviewers note that 'MVPA (like any other method) carries assumptions and limitations that should shape how the data are interpreted' and request this be discussed (Comment 9). They also note that 'a whole-brain MVPA mapping approach might well reveal other regions that code action preparation that are not activated (or not selectively activated) in the univariate sense' (Comment 8), indicating concern about methodological limitations and interpretation of null effects.

Reviewers raise multiple methodological concerns: they question whether 'the number of voxels across ROIs' was balanced, noting 'MVPA performance is strongly influenced by the number of voxels tested' (Comment 6); they request control analysis visualization for 'decoding of the ventricle and outside of the brain' to address 'a really insidious issue' (Comment 3); and they note that averaging cross-decoding directions may miss 'asymmetries in action coding' (Comment 7). These concerns indicate uncertainty about methodological rigor.

comparisons.notes: Perfect claim overlap (C48, C49) but strong disagreement. LLM finds auditory control analysis sufficient to rule out cue confounds. Peer reviewers express critical concern that auditory cues were identical across effectors and could be 'responsible for some or even all of the apparently cross-effector classification,' stating 'this issue must be addressed.'

Perfect claim overlap (C46, C47) with agreement on uncertainty. Both acknowledge lack of consistent voxel-level topography. LLM notes this limits mechanistic interpretation; peer reviewers request voxel-wise weight analysis to reconcile seemingly contradictory findings about whether different voxel populations drive different decoding effects.

High overlap (C24-C30, 7 shared claims) on experimental design and methodology. LLM finds methods appropriate and well-documented. Peer reviewers raise multiple methodological concerns: voxel number balancing across ROIs, need for control analyses in ventricles/outside brain, and potential asymmetries in cross-decoding directions, indicating uncertainty about methodological rigor.

Strong overlap (C35-C37, 3 shared claims) on time-resolved decoding. LLM finds temporal dynamics well-demonstrated and supportive of motor intention interpretation. Peer reviewers note lack of discussion about how decoding effects develop over time and request clarification on MVPA assumptions and limitations, indicating uncertainty about temporal interpretation.

Good overlap (C76, C77, C83, C88, C99, 5 shared claims) on occipitotemporal motor planning findings. Both agree these findings are well-supported. LLM emphasizes coupling between perceptual selectivity and motor planning. Peer reviewers note findings 'resonate with' connectivity-based explanations and encourage deeper theoretical development.

Moderate overlap (C42, C43, C45, 3 shared claims) on statistical comparisons and effector-specific findings. Both agree these results are well-supported. Peer reviewers describe them as 'a really important aspect of the findings' but note they are 'somewhat buried' in presentation, requesting better highlighting rather than questioning validity.

Partial overlap (C3, C22, C23, C41, 4 shared claims) on effector-independent coding. LLM finds hierarchical organization well-demonstrated. Peer reviewers find cross-effector decoding 'somewhat surprising' and request voxel-wise analysis to determine if different voxel populations drive these effects, expressing uncertainty about whether coding is genuinely effector-independent or reflects mixed populations.

Limited overlap (C19, C20, C38, C39, 4 shared claims) on hierarchical organization findings. Both agree on support for these claims. Peer reviewers acknowledge effector-specific findings as important while requesting improved presentation in Abstract and Introduction.

Minimal overlap (C2, C6, 2 shared claims) on main conclusions about hierarchical and distributed representations. Both agree these are supported. Peer reviewers describe work as 'excellent' and 'well-thought-out,' providing general endorsement of main conclusions despite specific methodological concerns about particular evidence.

Minimal overlap (C84, 1 shared claim) on mechanistic interpretations. LLM finds forward-state estimation role speculative requiring additional experiments. Peer reviewers support occipitotemporal findings broadly and encourage developing connectivity-based interpretations more fully. Different focus areas limit direct comparison.

Minimal overlap (C28, 1 shared claim) on delayed movement paradigm. LLM finds task design appropriate. Peer reviewers request more discussion of temporal dynamics and MVPA limitations. Limited shared claims make comprehensive comparison difficult.
